title: Julia Holter - Breaking and Entering
summary: Ahead of her concert at the Melbourne Recital Centre, acclaimed art-pop composer Julia Holter phoned in to speak with Charlie Miller about the inspirations behind her ambitious new album 'Aviary', as well as collaborating with Los Angeles-based composer Tashi Wada.
transcript:
Julia Holter spoke with Charlie Miller for Breaking and Entering in 2018, calling from Lausanne, Switzerland, to discuss Aviary, her Australian tour and her collaboration with Tashi Wada. Triple R dates the archived interview 17 January 2019. Edited for length and clarity.

Charlie: Where are you in the world right now?

Julia: I’m in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Charlie: You’ve recently been on a tour in Europe.

Julia: Right now I’m touring with the Tashi Wada group. We just finished my tour, and now we’re doing the Tashi Wada group tour. He had a show in Lausanne last night.

Charlie: His record is part of the FRKWYS series on RVNG Intl. What’s the process been like, playing with someone else on their tour? You probably haven’t done much of that in the last few years, touring so much with your own music.

Julia: It’s amazing. The travel part is more fun, actually, because it’s just three of us. I love playing his music. We have a lot more shows to do, so we’re just starting. It’s nice to think about someone else’s work and get caught up in that, especially because I love it so much.

Charlie: Tashi also performed on Aviary. You can hear his bagpipes on a number of the raging songs. Last time you were here, there were only four people on stage. It’s going to be different this time, I imagine.

Julia: There’s six of us, and Tashi’s in there. He’s playing synth and bagpipe. The other newer addition is trumpet. It’s electronic. The trumpet player also plays flugelhorn, which is similar to trumpet but a little different. It’s cool sometimes, the relationship between the bagpipe and the flugelhorn. There are a lot of really great things happening on stage, so I’m excited.

Charlie: Is that Sarah Belle Reid performing the trumpet?

Julia: Yeah.

Charlie: She was also on the recording. I love ‘Voce Simul’, and I believe it was just you two who recorded that song.

Julia: Yeah. Sorry, I’m at breakfast right now.

Charlie: What are you eating?

Julia: I’m eating muesli.

Charlie: That’s a pretty reliable option.

Charlie: You were collaborating with a lot of musicians on this record. How was it different to record ‘Voce Simul’ with just one person?

Julia: That was really special. I love that interaction, the contrast in approach with that song. It’s just two people, which is really nice. When we’ve performed it live, it’s been nice to have that moment of just two musicians playing, because it is a big group, at least for me.

Charlie: Six people is very serious, especially to tour as far as Australia.

Julia: Yeah, it’s exciting.

Charlie: When I’m listening to ‘Everyday Is an Emergency’, it takes on a sense of religious fervour. Did you listen to any spiritual music, perhaps not for that song in particular, but in creating Aviary?

Julia: I don’t have any religious connections at all, and I didn’t grow up with religion. But for whatever reason, I can be drawn to spiritual music. Maybe because, regardless of the religious context, which obviously is a very important part, there’s a sidestepping of intellectual justifications for things. Choral music obviously has this kind of power. I also like secular medieval music. I think there’s something to that sidestepping of justifying things. I also love Alice Coltrane’s devotional music, chant, more singing kind of music. I’ve noticed it’s not just me. A lot of people are really moved by sacred music, often without knowing the context, which I don’t know how people feel about, but I think it’s just the human thing. Maybe humans are spiritual. I don’t know anything about that. Just on a basic level, I think there’s music that can be very enveloping.

Charlie: On the last song, ‘Why Sad Song’, there’s a writing credit for Choying Drolma. Were you in communication with her, or was that a textual reference?

Julia: I made ‘Why Sad Song’ ten years ago. It’s very old. It’s a thing I used to do called phonetic translation, where I’d take the sound of a song and put it into English, instead of a meaning translation. I did that with the Choying Drolma track ‘Kyema Mimin’, and I did it with a lot of other things too. There are a few other credits on the album. That’s the one I’ve stuck with and been performing for a long time because it calms me. It’s very meditative. In doing that, it’s a very subjective process. I’m turning words into English, making these words that may or may not have anything, probably have nothing, to do with what Choying Drolma was chanting. I wanted to release it, and I was always scared to ask, because it’s basically a cover in a way, a cover of her recording. I wanted to ask her and Steve, who I think produced it, wrote or co— I don’t know, they made this track together. They approved it, very kindly. I was really happy after ten years of performing it to get approval, because I didn’t ever know if I would.

Charlie: You live in LA, and you’ve spoken about Blade Runner as a thematic influence on this record. Were you consciously thinking about the disconcerting fact that next year is the year in which the film takes place in LA?

Julia: Definitely. I was thinking about that. Maybe some real-world parallels are happening, things that were predicted in 1982, which is a little stressful.

Charlie: You’ve worked a lot with the visual artist Dicky Bahto. What exactly is the hand gesture you’re making on the album cover? Am I allowed to ask, or is it a secret?

Julia: It’s not a secret. I don’t know what it is. He was taking photos of me in the kitchen, and actually Tashi Wada was in some of those photos too. I think I was making a medieval kind of sign, almost jokingly.

Charlie: I don’t actually watch Star Trek, but it looks a lot like the Vulcan salute. I’m sure people have brought that up.

Julia: I’ve heard it’s the Star Trek sign. I don’t know that much about that. What does it mean?

Charlie: I think it means live long and prosper. I was looking it up yesterday.

Julia: That’s so good. That’s a good thing that it means.

Julia: That was definitely the vibe I was trying to give on this record.

Charlie: Down the bottom of the cover there are characters that look influenced by medieval scripture, but also have a galactic quality. What do they say? Is it the album name?

Julia: It’s not the album name. It’s actually a lyric from one of the songs. Some people have figured it out. I guess I could tell you, but it wouldn’t be as fun.

Charlie: I’ll go figure it out myself.

Julia: It’s Wingdings, a funny little font that I think most computers have. It’s really silly, just for fun. But it’s a meaningful lyric for me.

Charlie: When did you realise you had a tendency to draw on texts and art from all over the world and many different time periods?

Julia: I guess there was a point where I thought most art was like that. Maybe mine is more so like that, I’m not sure. Maybe ten years ago I started thinking about this because I was analysing how I write a little more. I was just starting to have a sense of what I was doing, and I still don’t have a sense of what I’m doing. I was interested in medieval stuff and didn’t really understand why, and I still don’t. There’s this thing, ‘Colligere’, which is a word that’s one of the titles of the songs on my record. I guess it means to collect and gather. I’m not necessarily answering your question, which is when. But around that time, ten years ago, I was thinking about how to explain my work, because I was in school, trying to explain myself all the time, which is really hard. That’s how I learnt to explain things: I’m collecting and gathering. I gather sounds, some of them my own, some found. To me, that’s just how I work. The word Colligere came out of this book talking about how memory was used in creative work in the Middle Ages, as a way to compose.

Charlie: That’s a process you’ve embraced in your own making?

Julia: Memory, if you think about it in a general sense, the past mixing with the present, there’s a collage quality to that in the mind as well. It’s hard to explain some of these things. I guess it was around that time I started thinking about my interest in collecting sounds and words. Especially with words, I find it more fun to borrow and do different things, like phonetic translation, to write words. Sometimes it’s more fun, like a gathering of different voices. A phonetic translation obviously isn’t a normal translation, but generating a new text from an old text is interesting in a way you can’t get just from your own subconscious. Although most of my songs are just my own words. Most of the songs on the record I wrote without any other text, so it’s a little much to say they’re all like that.

Charlie: For a while you’ve had this desire in your music to reach for the ecstatic, with Ekstasis named for that state of ecstasy. Do you feel you were able to do that on this album? Is that something you value in your songwriting?

Julia: I don’t know if I think about those moments as— Well, yeah, sometimes I do. I do value them.
